sec.title: Background
sec.p: Plant height (PH), as a key trait of plant architecture, is the embodiment of biomass accumulation and plays a critical role in determining wheat yield. Excavating diverse PH genes and understanding their pleiotropic effects on important agronomic traits are essential to enrich the PH gene pool and facilitate their further application in breeding.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: In this study, five stable PH QTLs were identified on chromosome 2B, 4A, 4B, 5A and 6A in a double haploid (DH) population from the cross between two elite wheat cultivars, Chuanmai 42 and Kechengmai 1. The QPh.cib-4B and QPh.cib-6A were major QTL and had a significant additive effect on PH. The QPh.cib-4B was confirmed as the Rht-B1, and QPh.cib-6A might be a new QTL. The major QTLs were further validated in different genetic backgrounds using the Kompetitive Allele-Specific PCR (KASP) markers. Using near-isogenic lines (NILs), QPh.cib-6A was demonstrated to pleiotropically increase plant height (PH), thousand grain weight (TGW), and spike length (SL) without negatively affecting grain number per spike (GNS) or spikelet number per spike (SNS). In contrast, QPh.cib-4B exhibited significant effects on PH but had no influence on TGW, GNS, SL, or SNS. Notably, the frequency of elite haplotype of QPh.cib-6A remains relatively low in Chinese wheat varieties. Thus, the combination of QPh.cib-4B and QPh.cib-6A represents a promising genetic module with considerable potential for high-yield wheat breeding. Expression analysis in NILs and sequence characterization identified TraesCS6A02G234400 and TraesCS6A02G235300 as the candidate genes for QPh.cib-6A.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This study identified five QTLs for PH in wheat. Two major QTLs were further validated in different genetic backgrounds, and their genetic effects on yield-related traits were analyzed in near-isogenic lines (NILs) to evaluate their potential in wheat breeding. Taken together, our results advance our understanding of the genetic basis for PH and enrich the PH QTL pool.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Bread wheat (Triticum aestivum L., AABBDD, 2n = 6x = 42), one of the most important food crops, provides about one-fifth of the calories used by humans around the world [1, 2]. However, with the impact of the growing global population, rapid climate change and water scarcity, ensuring global food security appears to be a pivotal challenge [3, 4].

Plant height (PH), as a key trait of plant architecture of wheat, is mainly determined by the stem length. Stem is the above-ground support organ, which has both function of “source” and “reservoir”, and is also the channel of “flow” between leaves and spike [5, 6]. Its morphology is closely associated with high yield and lodging resistance of wheat. Evidently, PH is not a yield component, but has a decisive impact on yield of wheat. Lodging resistance, mainly determined by PH and stem strength, is vital for wheat yield [1]. The wheat “Green Revolution” of the 1960s achieved a spectacular increase in wheat yield through introduction of the semi-dwarf genes Rht-B1b and Rht-D1b to reduce PH, enhancing lodging resistance and yield [7, 8]. However, excessively reducing PH is not recommended in breeding programs, as PH reflects biomass accumulation, and severe reduction often compromises maximum yield potential [1, 9, 10]. A more effective strategy may involve fine-tuning PH to an optimal level, which could enhance yield potential while maintaining lodging resistance. Thus, optimizing PH by introduction of diverse PH loci, especially those with rather minor effects on PH and pleiotropically positive effects on other agronomically important traits, is essential for developing high-yield wheat varieties.

To date, 27 reduced height genes (Rht1–Rht27) have been named in wheat [7, 11–13]. Rht1 (Rht-B1b) and Rht2 (Rht-D1b) encode DELLA protein, that increase wheat yield through reducing height to improve lodging resistance, but show short coleoptile, weak seedling vigor and frost susceptible. Rht3 (Rht-B1c), Rht11 (Rht-B1e) and Rht17 (Rht-B1p) are alleles of Rht-1, and Rht10 (Rht-D1c) is allele of Rht2 [14–16]. Rht8 encodes a ribonuclease H-Like 1 protein. It reduces PH by about 8% and significantly increase the grains number per spike (GNS), spikelet number per spike (SNS) and the grain yield [17, 18]. Rht18 and Rht24 are the same gene encoding GA2oxA09, which reduces PH by about 10% without affecting thousand grain weight (TGW) and yield [7, 19]. Rht12 encodes GA2oxA13, which reduces PH by about 46% and improves the fertility of spikelet, but delays the heading date [20, 21]. Rht23 encodes a AP2 transcription factor and is homologous to the Q gene, which significantly shortens the spike length (SL) while reducing PH [22]. Rht13 encodes a nucleotide-binding site/leucine-rich repeat (NB-LRR) protein. It reduces PH by about 17% without affecting yield [23]. Rht25 encodes a plant-specific A/T-rich sequence- and zinc-binding protein (PLATZ), and pleiotropically affects PH, coleoptile length and SL [24, 25]. In addition, some genes related to spike and spikelet development, environmental adaptation and domestication also pleiotropically regulate PH, such as Vrn-1, Ppd-1, Q, TaCol-B5, SVP1, TB1, TaCOLD1, TaCRY1, etc [26–33]. However, although many dwarfing genes have been identified, only the Rht-B1, Rht-D1, Rht8 and Rht18/24 have been widely utilized in wheat breeding currently [13].

Grain yield is a complex quantitative trait determined by multiple QTLs/genes, such that variation at a single locus would not be sufficient to cause substantial phenotypic changes [1]. Designing the ideal plant architecture by pyramiding multiple loci with complementary effects is a promising strategy for wheat high-yield breeding. Therefore, identifying new PH genetic loci and evaluating their genetic effects are essential to enrich the PH gene pool and facilitate their further application in breeding. In our previous study, a double haploidy (DH) population from the cross between two elite wheat cultivars, Chuanmai 42 (CM42) and Kechengmai 1 (K1) was developed, and a genetic linkage map based on Wheat 55 K SNP array was built [34]. In the present study, combining phenotypic analysis in multiple field trials, five chromosomal regions controlling PH were identified. Two major QTLs, QPh.cib-6A and QPh.cib-4B, were further validated in different genetic backgrounds by developing Kompetitive Allele Specific PCR (KASP) markers, and their genetic effects on yield-related traits were analyzed in near-isogenic lines (NILs) to evaluate their potential in wheat breeding. Moreover, the distribution frequency of QPh.cib-6A was analyzed in Chinese wheat varieties, and its candidate genes were also predicted.

sec.title: Plant materials and field trials
sec.p: The 189 DH lines (CK1) derived from the cross of CM42×K1 were developed for QTL mapping (Figure S1). The other two bi-parental populations, including a DH population derived from the cross of CM42×Kechengmai 4 (K4, CK4) and a F7 RIL population derived from the cross of K1×K4 (KK), were employed to validate the major QTL in different genetic backgrounds (Figure S1). The NILs for the defined major QTL were developed with CM42 as the donor parent and K1 as the recurrent parent. Heterozygous plants were selected at each generation using the KASP markers for marker-assisted backcrossing. After four generations (BC4) of backcrossing and self-crossing two times, the BC4F3 populations with different homozygous segments of the target QTL interval were selected to analyze the gene expression and effects on yield-related traits (Figure S1). A wheat germplasm panel consisted of 250 bread wheat varieties and collected from the major wheat production regions of China were used for haplotype analysis, including 102 from the Northern Winter Wheat Zone, 88 from the Yellow and Huai River Valleys Facultative Wheat Zone, 37 from the Southwest Wheat Zone, and 23 from the Mid-lower Reaches of the Yangtze River Valley Wheat Zone (Figure S1).

The trials were performed with a randomized block design on the experimental farm of Shifang (SHF, 104˚11’E, 31˚6’N) and Shuangliu (SHL, 103˚52’E, 30˚34’N) in Sichuan Province, China. Each line of the populations was planted in a five-row plot with a row length of 2.0 m with 50 seeds per row, at a row spacing of 0.3 m. Field management and disease control were performed according to the common practices for wheat production.

sec.title: Phenotypic evaluation and statistical analysis
sec.p: For each plot, 10 representative plants in the center of each row were randomly selected to measure PH, SL and SNS at physiological maturity before harvest. Subsequently, main spikes of all selected plants were harvested, and manually threshed for evaluating TGW, GNS, grain width (GW) and grain length (GL) by SC-G software (WSeen, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China). PH is the length from the ground to the tip of spike excluding the awns, and was measured in the field using a ruler; SL is the length from the base of the rachis to the terminal spikelet excluding awns, and SNS is determined by counting the number of spikelet per spike. For The CK1 population, phenotypes were measured in the wheat-growing seasons of 2017–2018 (E1), 2018–2019 (E2) and 2019–2020 (E4) at SHF, and 2018–2019 (E3) and 2019–2020 (E5) at SHL, and that of CK4, KK and natural populations was measured in E2, E3, E4 and E5. For the NILs, phenotypes were measured in the wheat-growing seasons of 2021–2022 at SHF (E6) and SHL (E7). Weather conditions of the field trails during the wheat growth stage were listed in the Table S1.

Best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP) data which was used for combined QTL detection, correlation analyses, and effect analysis were calculated by using the R package “lme4” (https://github.com/lme4/lme4). Phenotypic correlations, frequency distribution and Student t test were computed in SPSS v20 software (IBM SPSS, Armonk, USA). Broad-sense heritability (H2) was calculated using the function of ANOVA in the ICI mapping software (https://isbreedingen.caas.cn/news1/software22/294519.htm) with the following formula: , where represents the genotype variance, represents the variance of genotype by environmental effect, represents the variance by environmental effect, represents the residual variance, n is the number of environments, and r is the number of replicates [35].

sec.title: QTL analysis
sec.p: A whole-genome genetic map of the CK1 population was previously constructed using the Wheat 55 K SNP array data that contains 2409 bin markers and spans 3091.39 cM across the 21 chromosomes of wheat [34]. Here, an integrated genetic linkage map containing seven KASP markers that are linked with the major QTLs/genes detected previously was used for QTL mapping (Table S2). Among the KASP markers, KASP_AX-110,462,709 and KASP_AX-109,308,935 are closely linked with two major SL QTLs, QSc/Sl.cib-5A and QSc/Sl.cib-6A, respectively; KASP_AX-111,241,476 is closely linked with a major GL QTL, QGl.cib-4A; KASP_AX-108,941,085 is closely linked with a major GW and TGW QTL, GTgw/Gw.cib-4B; KASP_Vrn-A1 is located in the intron region of Vrn-A1, and KASP_Rht1 is located near to the Rht1 (Rht-B1) [36, 37].

QTL analysis in individual environment was performed by using the inclusive composite interval mapping (ICIM) function in the Biparental Populations (BIP) module of the IciMapping v4.2 software [35]. The parameter was set as following: walking step = 1 cM, PIN = 0.005, and logarithm of odds (LOD) = 3. The Met (multi-environmental trials) and EPI functional module were utilized to detect interactions between environments and QTLs and epistatic effects between two loci, respectively, with the parameters setting as PIN = 0.001, Step = 1 cM, LOD = 5 [35, 38]. QTL that was stably identified in at least four environments and BLUP data with explaining greater than 10% of phenotypic variation was considered major.

sec.title: Validation and effects of major QTLs
sec.p: On the basis of QTL mapping results, the flanking markers of each QTL were positioned onto the Chinese Spring (CS) genome assembly (IWGSC RefSeq v1.0) for identifying their physical positions. The KASP markers within the physical intervals of major QTL were developed for tracking the target genomic regions according to the methods described by Li et al. [39]. CK4 and KK populations were employed to validate the effect of the major QTL on PH in different genetic backgrounds. The NILs were developed for evaluating the effects of the major QTLs on PH and other yield-related traits.

sec.title: Haplotype analysis
sec.p: KASP markers spanning the target interval of major QTL were developed and used to genotype the 250 Chinese wheat varieties, which were classified into ‘CM42-like’ haplotype (H-CM42) and ‘K1-like’ haplotype (H-K1) based on their genotypes. The frequency distribution and difference in PH of the two haplotypes were analyzed.

sec.title: Prediction of the candidate genes for QPh.cib-6A
sec.p: Genes within the target interval were extracted based on the annotation of CS genome (IWGSC Refseq v1.1 annotation), and functionally annotated using the Uniprot (https://www.uniprot.org/). The sequence variation of candidate gene was analyzed between parental lines based on the whole-genome sequencing data of CM42 and K1 that were previously generated using the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform [39]. Moreover, the stem internodes from the NIL pairs of QPh.cib-6A collected at jointing and heading stage were subjected to RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) for gene expression analysis with three independent biological replicates. The RNA-seq libraries prepared with a Poly-A Purificati on TruSeq Library Prep Kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform were performed by Biomarker Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). After quality controlling, clean reads were mapped to IWGSC RefSeq v1.0. The expression level of genes was calculated using fragments per kb per million (FPKM) [40]. The Raw sequencing reads has been deposited with ID CRA023932 at the China National Center for Bioinformation (https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/gsa/).

sec.title: Phenotypic evaluation
sec.p: PH of the CK1 population and parents were evaluated in five environments (Table S3). As shown in the Table 1, significant difference in PH between CM42 and K1 was observed in three environments. In the CK1 population, PH among all environments and the BLUP data showed wide phenotypic variability with the coefficient of variation (CV) ranging from 13.29 to 16.52% (Table 1). ANOVA analysis showed that PH was significantly affected (P < 0.001) by genotype, environment and genotype×environment interaction (Table S4). However, there was a high broad-sense heritability estimate (H2 = 0.95), suggesting that PH was stable and mainly determined by genetic factors (Table 1). This conclusion was further supported by the significantly positive correlation (P < 0.001) for PH among all environments and the BLUP data (r = 0.79–0.98) (Fig. 2a). Moreover, PH followed a normal distribution with a transgressive segregation in all environments and the BLUP data, indicating that the PH was quantitatively controlled by multiple genes and the favorable alleles are present in both parents (Fig. 1; Table 1). Pairwise correlations between PH and other yield-related traits were calculated using the BLUP data and showed that PH was positively correlated with TGW, GW and SL, negatively correlated with the SC, and not correlated with GL, GNS and SNS, respectively. These results indicated that PH may have pleiotropic effects on yield-related traits (Fig. 2b).

sec.title: QTL analysis in individual environment
sec.p: Using the ICIM-BIP method, a total of 5 additive QTLs for PH were detected on chromosomes 2B, 4A, 4B, 5A and 6A in at least three environments. Each QTL explained 2.33–25.05% of variation in the PH with the LOD values ranging from 3.69 to 27.37 (Table 2). QPh.cib-4B, QPh.cib-5A and QPh.cib-6A were detected in all environments and the BLUP data, explaining 4.37–25.05%, 4–21.38% and 4.53–15.69% of the phenotypic variation, respectively. QPh.cib-2B was detected in three environments and the BLUP data and explained 5.4–7.73% of the phenotypic variation. QPh.cib-4A was detected in four environments and explained 2.33–5.72% of the phenotypic variation. However, only QPh.cib-4B and QPh.cib-6A had average PVE values higher than 10%, suggesting that they were major loci for PH with relative larger effect (Table 2).

sec.p: Based on the mapping results, we further evaluated the effect of these QTLs on PH in the CK1 population. As shown in the Fig. 3, the allele from CM42 increased PH by 4.26-6.8%, 6.78-8.76% and 8.22-11.02% at QPh.cib-2B, QPh.cib-5A and QPh.cib-6A, respectively, and decreased PH by 6.69-7.66% and 8.65-15.33% at QPh.cib-4A and QPh.cib-4B, respectively (Fig. 3).

sec.title: QTL-by-environment interaction analysis
sec.p: Using the ICIM-MET method, five QTLs same as these detected in individual environment were identified, that had the PVE (A) values (phenotypic variation explained by additive and dominance) ranging from 1.2 to 15.41%, and the PVE (AbyE) values (phenotypic variation explained by additive and dominance by environment effect) ranging from 0.21 to 5% (Table S5). Except for QPh.cib-5A, PVE (AbyE) of the other four QTLs were low, indicating that they were less affected by the environmental factors (Table S5). Remarkably, PVE (A) of the two major QTLs was high, with 15.41% for QPh.cib-4B and 8.29% for QPh.cib-6A, while PVE (AbyE) was low, with 0.62% for QPh.cib-4B and 0.21% for QPh.cib-6A. The results further indicated that QPh.cib-4B and QPh.cib-6A were less influenced by environmental factors and can be stably expressed (Table S5).

sec.title: Epistatic analysis
sec.p: Epistasis is an important and complex component of quantitative genetics. In this study, five epistatic QTLs (eQTLs) for PH were detected in 2018SHF, 2019SHF, 2019SHL and the BLUP data, explaining 2.79–12.14% of the phenotypic variation (Table S6). However, none of eQTLs was overlapped with these QTLs detected in the ICIM-BIP analysis, suggesting that these eQTLs indirectly influence the phenotype through interactions with each other.

sec.title: Pyramiding of the major QTL
sec.p: Pyramiding major QTLs or genes is a powerful tool to improve complex traits. In this study, the alleles that increase PH at the major QTL QPh.cib-4B and QPh.cib-6A were contributed by K1 and CM42, respectively. Thus, we further analyzed their additive effect. As shown in the Fig. 4, pyramiding of the two major QTLs had a significant additive effect and decreased PH by 17.93-25.22% in the CK1 population.

sec.title: Validation of the major QTL in different genetic backgrounds
sec.p: Among the major QTL, QPh.cib-4B was closely linked with the KASP-Rht1 which was located near to the Rht1 and detected polymorphism between K4 and K1. QPh.cib-6A was located between AX-109,999,937 and AX-109,353,146, corresponding to the physical interval of 442.4 Mb-445.41 Mb (Table 2). The KASP marker, KASP_442.04, located near to this interval was successfully developed and detected polymorphism between CM42 and K4 (Table S7). Thus, the KK and CK4 populations were employed to validate the QPh.cib-4B and QPh.cib-6A, respectively, in different genetic backgrounds. As expected, the allele from K1 at QPh.cib-4B could significantly increase PH by 13.03-14.14% in the KK population (Fig. 5a), and the allele from CM42 at QPh.cib-6A could significantly increase PH by 7.52-8.82% in the CK4 population (Fig. 5b).

sec.title: Genetic effects of the major QTL on PH and yield-related traits
sec.p: NILs are ideal materials for accurately analyzing the genetic effects of single QTL due to less genetic background noise (Table S8). In the NILs of QPh.cib-6A, the allele from CM42 significantly increased PH by 17.26-26.78% and TGW by 8.56-12.09% without affecting SNS. For the GNS and SL, effects of QPh.cib-6A were environmentally sensitive, but the allele from CM42 did not reduce GNS and SL (Fig. 6a, c). In the NILs of QPh.cib-4B, the allele of CM42 significantly reduced PH by 12.46-20.6% without penalty on SL, SNS, TGW, and GNS (Fig. 6b, d).

sec.title: Haplotype analysis in the interval of QPh.cib-6A
sec.p: Haplotype analysis of the QPh.cib-6A was conducted using a wheat natural population consisting of 250 wheat varieties. KASP_442.04 and KASP_452.06 were used to trace the target genomic region of QPh.cib-6A (Fig. 7a). Of the 250 wheat varieties, 140 (56%) and 110 (44%) carried the haplotype of CM42 (Hap-CM42) and K1 (Hap-K1), respectively (Fig. 7c). Effect analysis showed that varieties carrying the Hap-CM42 had higher PH (9.96-13.37%) than those carrying the Hap-K1, which further verified the association of the two haplotypes with PH (Fig. 7a). Moreover, the frequencies of Hap-CM42 were 76.47%, 45.45%, 45.95% and 21.74% in the Northern Winter Wheat Zone, Yellow and Huai River Valleys Facultative Wheat Zone, Southwest Wheat Zone, and Mid-lower Reaches of the Yangtze River Valley Wheat Zone, respectively (Fig. 7c).

sec.title: Candidate gene prediction for QPh.cib-6A
sec.p: QPh.cib-6A was mapped in an interval between 442.4 Mb and 445.41 Mb of chromosome arm 6AL of CS genome containing 17 predicted genes. Sequence variation analysis showed that eight non-synonymous single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were found in five of these genes, including TraesCS6A02G234400, TraesCS6A02G235300, TraesCS6A02G235500, TraesCS6A02G235600 and TraesCS6A02G235700 (Table S9). Furthermore, transcriptome analysis showed that only TraesCS6A02G234400 and TraesCS6A02G235300 had significant differences in expression between NIL-CM42QPh.cib−6A and NIL-K1QPh.cib−6A in the stem internodes of jointing and heading stage (Table S9). The results suggested that TraesCS6A02G234400 and TraesCS6A02G235300 may be related to plant growth and development, and are the key candidate genes of QPh.cib-6A.

sec.title: Correlation analysis of PH and yield-related traits
sec.p: PH, as a key trait of plant architecture, is the important embodiment of the plant biomass accumulation and closely related to wheat yield. In this study, the significant positive correlation between PH, and GW and TGW was detected, indicating that the increase of biomass may be conducive to grain filling and, ultimately, increase grain weight. No correlation between PH, and GNS and SNS was detected, suggesting that the increase of PH had no effect on the development of wheat spikelet. SL, as a component of PH, is positively correlated with PH, which is consistent with the results of this study. Moreover, lodging, closely related to PH, is the primary problem to overcome in the high-yield wheat breeding. Thus, under the premise of maintaining lodging resistance, appropriately increasing PH may be an effective strategy to overcome the trade-off between TGW and GNS, and then improve wheat yield.

sec.title: Comparison with QTLs/genes of PH identified in previous studies
sec.p: To further clarify relationships between QTLs detected in this study and those reported in previous studies, we compared their physical intervals corresponding to CS reference genome. QPh.cib-2B was located in the interval between 778.18 Mb and 779.68 Mb on chromosome arm 2BL (Table 2), which is physically close to the TaARF12-2B at 775.72 Mb [41, 42]. Thus whether they are the same locus needs to be confirmed by subsequent fine mapping and map-based cloning. QPh.cib-4A was located in the interval between 45.48 Mb and 102.84 Mb on chromosome arm 4AS (Table 2), which was overlapped with Qph.ccshau-4A, and close to QHT.uia2.4A-1, suggesting that they are likely the same locus [43, 44]. For the QPh.cib-4B, it was closely linked with the marker KASP_Rht1, and overlapped with Pht.Sparc-4B, QPht.dms-4B, QPH.caas-4BS.2 and QPh.cau-4B.2 [45–48]. Sequence difference analysis showed that CM42 carries the Rht-B1b, while K1 carries the allele Rht-B1i (a single missense SNP, A614G, in the coding region resulting in Glu205Gly substitution), indicating that the QPh.cib-4B is likely the Rht-B1 (Figure S2). QPh.cib-5A was located in the interval between 535.53 Mb and 540.06 Mb on chromosome arm 5AL (Table 2), where no QTL for PH have been identified previously. Rht9 on chromosome 5A is closely linked to the BARC151 at 560.13 Mb [49], which is physically separated from QPh.cib-5A, suggesting that QPh.cib-5A may be a novel PH QTL. QPh.cib-6A was located in the interval between 442.4 Mb and 445.41 Mb on chromosome arm 6AL (Table 2). Several Rht genes have been identified on chromosome 6A, with Rht18 and Rht24 being alleles locating at 416.23 Mb, and Rht25 at 148.39 Mb on 6AS, respectively [7, 20]. They are physically separated from QPh.cib-6A. Moreover, no reported QTL for PH was overlapped with QPh.cib-6A, thus QPh.cib-6A may be a novel QTL.

sec.title: Genetic effects of QPh.cib-4B and QPh.cib-6A and their application in molecular breeding programs
sec.p: In this study, by constructing the NILs of QPh.cib-4B and QPh.cib-6A, we accurately evaluated their genetic effects on yield-related traits. QPh.cib-6A showed pleiotropic and positive effects on PH, TGW and SL, but had no effect on GNS and SNS (Fig. 6c). Notably, QPh.cib-6A did not penalize GNS for an increase in TGW, suggesting that it may be a valuable QTL capable of breaking the trade-off between GNS and TGW (Fig. 6c). However, the increased PH simultaneously increases the risk of lodging, which is undesirable for yield improvement in wheat breeding. For the QPh.cib-4B, it had a significant effect on PH, but not on TGW, GNS, SL and SNS, indicating that it has application potential in dwarf breeding (Fig. 6d). Wheat yield is a complex trait, and it is difficult to achieve the desired breeding goal by relying on a single locus for genetic improvement. Pyramiding QTL/gene with complementary effects provides an effective approach to optimize their positive roles in improvement of wheat yield. Given there was a significant additive effect on PH for QPh.cib-6A and QPh.cib-4B, the lodging risk brought by QPh.cib-6A may be attenuated or eliminated by polymerization with QPh.cib-4B (Fig. 4). In addition, the frequency of QPh.cib-6A elite haplotype is relatively low in the Yellow and Huai River Valleys Facultative Wheat Zone, Southwest Wheat Zone, and Mid-lower Reaches of the Yangtze River Valley Wheat Zone of China (Fig. 7c). Thus, the major QTLs and KASP markers reported here may have great potential for high-yield wheat breeding.

sec.title: Analysis of candidate genes for QPh.cib-6A
sec.p: Within the physical interval of QPh.cib-6A, there were 17 predicted genes in the CS genome. Analysis of these genes, including their expression patterns, annotations, and sequence variation, indicated that TraesCS6A02G234400 and TraesCS6A02G235300 may be related to plant growth. TraesCS6A02G234400 encodes a BRO1 domain-containing protein, which modulates recruitment of FREE1 to the MVB/PVC membrane by competitively binding to the endosomal sorting complex required for transport component VPS23. It plays essential roles in vacuole formation, endosomal sorting of plasma membrane proteins, and auxin/abscisic acid-mediated plant growth and development [50–52]. TraesCS6A02G235300 encodes a protein serine/threonine phosphatase and has been shown to be key negative regulator of abscisic acid signalling pathways and regulate plant growth and development [53, 54]. Sugimoto et al. reported that the overexpression of type2C protein serine/threonine phosphatase (PP2C) enhanced the plant biomass production by increasing inflorescence stem growth in Arabidopsis [55]. OsPP2C09, a negative regulatory factor in abscisic acid signalling, plays an essential role in balancing plant growth and drought tolerance, and the overexpression of the OsPP2C09 significantly increased the PH, panicle length, TGW, and biomass production of rice [56]. In general, these findings provide a foundation for the subsequent fine mapping and map-based cloning of QPh.cib-6A and enhance our knowledge of the genetic basis for PH in wheat.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this study, five stable PH QTLs were identified. The major QTL QPh.cib-4B and QPh.cib-6A were further validated in different genetic backgrounds using the KASP markers. The QPh.cib-4B was confirmed as Rht-B1 and QPh.cib-6A may be a new QTL. QPh.cib-6A was demonstrated to pleiotropically increase PH, TGW, and SL without negatively affecting GNS or SNS. In contrast, QPh.cib-4B exhibited significant effects on PH but had no influence on TGW, GNS, SL, or SNS. Notably, the frequency of elite haplotype of QPh.cib-6A remains relatively low in Chinese wheat varieties. Moreover, expression analysis in NILs and sequence characterization identified the candidate genes for QPh.cib-6A.
